choices: It raises an IndexError
It prints blue
It prints red
It prints 3
python.explanation: `len(colors)` is 3, so this asks for `colors[3]`. The valid indexes are 0, 1, and 2, so index 3 is one step past the end and Python raises an IndexError. If you picked "blue", you reasoned that the length points at the last item, which is the exact assumption that causes this error. To get "blue", subtract one: `colors[len(colors) - 1]`, or just write `colors[-1]`.

java.prompt: Which of these describes what Java does with this code?
choices: It prints 0 and 3, then throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
It prints 0, 3, and done, because assigning to scores[3] grows the array
It refuses to compile, because slot 3 does not exist
It prints nothing, because the array was never filled in
java.explanation: The first two lines are fine: an int array starts full of zeros, so `scores[0]` is 0, and `scores.length` is 3. Then `scores[3] = 99` asks for slot 3 when the only slots are 0, 1, and 2. Java throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and stops, so "done" never prints. The compile error is a tempting pick, but an index is a value the program works out while running, so Java cannot judge it in advance and only finds out when it arrives there. Assigning past the end never grows an array. The size was fixed the moment you wrote `new int[3]`.

python.prompt: This code is trying to delete every 2. It prints `[1, 3, 2]`. Why is a 2 still there?
choices: Removing an item shifts the rest left, so the loop steps over the item that moved into the gap
`.remove()` only ever deletes one item, no matter how many times you call it
The loop ends early because the list got shorter than it started
`.remove()` cannot delete numbers, only strings
python.explanation: The loop keeps its place by position. It checks position 1, finds a 2, and removes it. Everything after that slides one step to the left, but the loop still advances to position 2, so the 2 that just moved into position 1 is never looked at. `.remove()` worked fine every time you called it, which is why the second choice is tempting and still wrong. The real problem is that you changed the list out from under the loop. Loop over the list to decide what to keep, and put those items in a new list.

java.prompt: `names` is an `ArrayList<String>` holding two names. Which line prints 2?
choices: `System.out.println(names.size());`
`System.out.println(names.length);`
`System.out.println(names.length());`
`System.out.println(len(names));`
java.explanation: An ArrayList counts with `size()`. The tempting answer is `names.length`, because you just learned that arrays use `length` and an ArrayList feels like the same sort of thing. It is not, and the compiler says so: "cannot find symbol: variable length". `names.length()` fails for the same reason, since `length()` belongs to String. Sort them by what you are holding: array uses `length`, String uses `length()`, ArrayList uses `size()`. As for `len(names)`, that is Python, and Java will not recognize it at all.

python.prompt: What job does a Python list do?
choices: It stores many values under one name while keeping their order.
It stores only one value and replaces it every time.
It fixes index errors before the code runs.
It turns every stored value into text.
python.explanation: A list holds several values in order, written in square brackets: `scores = [88, 92, 75]`. You reach an item by its position, and positions start at 0, so `scores[0]` is the first one. `len(scores)` tells you how many items there are. Because counting starts at 0, the last valid position is always one less than the length. Lists can change after you make them: `.append(x)` adds to the end, `.pop()` removes the last item, and `.remove(x)` removes the first item equal to x.

java.prompt: How are Java arrays and ArrayLists different?
choices: An array has a fixed size; an ArrayList can grow as items are added.
An array grows automatically; an ArrayList is always fixed size.
Both use length() to count their items.
Both can store primitive int values in the same way.
java.explanation: An array holds a fixed number of values of one type: `int[] nums = new int[5];` reserves exactly 5 slots, and that size never changes. Positions start at 0, so the last valid index is `nums.length - 1`. On an array, `length` is a field, so it takes no parentheses. When you do not know the count ahead of time, use an `ArrayList`, which grows as you add to it: `add` puts an item on the end, `get(i)` reads one, `size()` counts them. An ArrayList holds objects, so a list of whole numbers is `ArrayList<Integer>`, never `ArrayList<int>`.

javascript.prompt: What job does a JavaScript array do?
choices: It stores ordered values that can be read by index.
It stores only one value and replaces it every time.
It prevents out-of-range indexes from ever happening.
It turns every stored value into text.
javascript.explanation: Arrays hold ordered values with zero-based indexes. `.length` gives the count, `.push(value)` adds at the end, and `.pop()` removes the final item.

cpp.prompt: What job does a C++ vector do?
choices: It stores ordered elements and can grow with push_back.
It stores only one value and replaces it every time.
It makes every index access checked by default.
It turns every stored value into text.
cpp.explanation: A fixed array has a compile-time size, while `std::vector` can grow. Vector indexes start at zero, `.size()` returns the count, and `.push_back` appends.

python.prompt: What does this print, and why?
choices: [1, 3, 2] — removing while looping makes the loop skip items
[1, 3] — every 2 is removed
[1, 2, 2, 3, 2] — remove does nothing inside a loop
It raises an error
python.explanation: Deleting from a list while looping over it shifts later items back by one, and the loop's position still moves forward, so it steps past the item that slid into the gap. Two of the 2s get skipped and survive, leaving [1, 3, 2]. Build a new list instead of mutating the one you are iterating.

choices: Prints 4, 7, 2, then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at i = 3
Prints 4, 7, 2 and stops cleanly
Prints 4, 7, 2, 0
Fails to compile
java.explanation: `<=` lets `i` reach 3, but an array of length 3 has valid indexes 0, 1, 2. `arr[3]` was never allocated, so after printing all three items Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The length is always one past the last index, so the correct guard is `i < arr.length`.

javascript.prompt: After this runs, what is in the original `courses` array?
choices: Unchanged — planned is a separate copy
It also gains "CS 301"
It becomes empty
It throws, because arrays cannot be spread
javascript.explanation: `[...courses]` builds a new array with the same items, so `planned` and `courses` are independent. Pushing to `planned` does not touch `courses`. Assigning `const planned = courses` (no spread) would share one array, and then the push would show up in both.

cpp.prompt: How does `scores.at(index)` differ from `scores[index]` when `index` is out of range?
choices: at() throws std::out_of_range; [] is undefined behavior
They behave identically
at() returns 0; [] returns -1
at() is invalid syntax on a vector
cpp.explanation: `at()` checks the bound and throws `std::out_of_range` on a bad index, so the failure is visible. `operator[]` does not check and reads invalid memory, which is undefined behavior and may not crash right away. Prefer `at()` when the index might be out of range.

python.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 1
python.prompt: A list has 4 items. Which statement about its indexes is true?
choices: Length is 4, and the last valid index is 3.
Length is 4, so the last valid index is also 4.
The first item is at index 1.
Python adds a blank slot when you ask for index 4.
python.explanation: Python list indexes start at 0. Four items occupy positions 0, 1, 2, and 3, so scores[4] reaches one past the end and raises IndexError.

java.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 1
java.prompt: How do you read the length of a Java array?
choices: Use `scores.length`, because array length is a field.
Use `scores.length()`, because arrays count with a method.
Use `scores.size()`, because arrays and ArrayLists share one API.
Use `len(scores)`, because Java borrows Python's count function.
java.explanation: Java arrays expose length as a field, so scores.length is correct. ArrayList uses size(), and String uses length(), which is why this small API difference is easy to mix up.

javascript.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 1
javascript.prompt: What does const mean for a JavaScript array variable?
choices: You cannot assign a different array to the variable, but you can still mutate the array.
The array is frozen, so push and pop throw errors.
Every item inside the array becomes read-only.
The array length can never change.
javascript.explanation: const protects the variable binding, not the array contents. You cannot point the name at a new array, but methods such as push can still change the current array.

cpp.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 1
cpp.prompt: What can happen when C++ vector code reads past the end with brackets?
choices: It causes undefined behavior, so the program may appear to work or fail unpredictably.
It always throws std::out_of_range.
It automatically grows the vector.
It returns 0 for the missing element.
cpp.explanation: operator[] does not check bounds on a vector. Stay below size(), or use at() when you want an out-of-range index to throw a visible exception.

python.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 2
python.prompt: In Python list code, how are `remove` and `pop` different?
choices: remove looks for a value; pop removes by position.
remove deletes by position; pop searches for a matching value.
Both remove and pop always delete the final item.
Both methods return a brand-new list.
python.explanation: tasks.remove("code") searches for the first matching value and deletes it. tasks.pop(1) deletes the item at index 1. Mixing value and position is the common mistake.

java.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 2
java.prompt: Why does Java require `ArrayList<Integer>` instead of `ArrayList<int>`?
choices: ArrayList stores objects, so whole numbers use the wrapper type Integer.
ArrayList can only store strings.
int values are allowed only in fixed arrays.
Integer makes the ArrayList fixed-size.
java.explanation: Java generics work with object types. int is primitive, so ArrayList<int> is invalid. Use ArrayList<Integer>, and Java will box and unbox many simple values for you.

javascript.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 2
javascript.prompt: Which indexing habit is reliable for JavaScript arrays?
choices: Start at index 0, and use length - 1 for the final item.
Start at index 1, and use length for the final item.
Use -1 to read the final item with bracket indexing.
Treat every missing index as an error that stops the program.
javascript.explanation: JavaScript array indexes begin at 0. If an array has length 3, the final item is at index 2, so length - 1 is the safe last-index calculation.

cpp.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 2
cpp.prompt: What must C++ code include before using std::vector?
choices: Include the vector header.
Include the array length inside square brackets.
Include a manual resize before every read.
Include no header because vector is built into the language.
cpp.explanation: std::vector is provided by the vector header. After including it, vector gives you size(), push_back(), at(), and bracket indexing.

python.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 3
python.prompt: A list result is missing neighboring items or is off by one. What should you check first?
choices: Whether an index is off by one or the list changed during the loop.
Whether the list should have been converted into a string first.
Whether every value in the list has the same type.
Whether print changed the list while displaying it.
python.explanation: Missing neighboring items often points to changing the list while looping. One-too-short or one-too-long results often point to an off-by-one boundary. Start by checking those two places.

java.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 3
java.prompt: Which statement about Java compile errors is true?
choices: Java catches type and member mistakes before the program runs.
Java catches every out-of-range array index before the program runs.
Java waits until printing before checking variable types.
Java treats compile errors as warnings and keeps running.
java.explanation: ArrayList<int> and nums.length() fail while Java compiles because the type or member does not exist. Out-of-range indexes are different: they usually fail at runtime.

javascript.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 3
javascript.prompt: How do you calculate the final JavaScript array index?
choices: Read an item before checking whether the collection is empty.
Skip the last item because the loop stops one position too early.
Use array.length - 1.
Visit one extra position because the loop uses `<=` with the length.
javascript.explanation: length is a count, not an index. The final index is one less than the count because array positions begin at 0.

cpp.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 3
cpp.prompt: Where does C++ vector indexing begin?
choices: Read an item before checking whether the collection is empty.
Skip the last item because the loop stops one position too early.
Begin at index 0.
Visit one extra position because the loop uses `<=` with the length.
cpp.explanation: std::vector indexes start at 0. A vector with size 3 has valid indexes 0, 1, and 2, so size() itself is already past the end.

python.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 4
python.prompt: How do you read the last item of a nonempty Python list?
choices: Use `lst[-1]`, or use `lst[len(lst) - 1]`.
Use `lst[len(lst)]`, because length names the final slot.
Use `lst[1]`, because the last item is counted after the first.
Use `lst[0]`, because Python stores the final item first.
python.explanation: The last zero-based index is len(lst) - 1. Python also gives you lst[-1] as a direct shortcut for the final item, as long as the list is not empty.

javascript.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 4
javascript.prompt: When should JavaScript code use push or pop?
choices: Copy only the variable name and assume a fresh list was created.
Mutate shared list data when independent plans are needed.
Sort the list before preserving the original order.
Use push to add at the end and pop to remove from the end.
javascript.explanation: push mutates the array by adding one item at the end. pop mutates the array by removing and returning the final item. Use them when changing the same array is intended.

cpp.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 4
cpp.prompt: Which C++ vector index is always out of range?
choices: Copy only the variable name and assume a fresh list was created.
Mutate shared list data when independent plans are needed.
Sort the list before preserving the original order.
The index equal to values.size().
cpp.explanation: For a vector with size n, valid indexes are 0 through n - 1. That means values[values.size()] is one past the end.

python.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 5
python.prompt: When is `for item in lst:` the right Python loop shape?
choices: Use it when the loop only needs each value, not the index.
Use nested indexes without checking the inner list length.
Assume every list method returns the changed list.
Append to the wrong list while building a result.
python.explanation: If the loop only needs the values, looping directly over the list avoids index math. Use indexes only when position matters.

java.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 5
java.prompt: Which Java loop boundary visits every array item once?
choices: Start at i = 0 and keep going while i < arr.length.
Use nested indexes without checking the inner list length.
Assume every list method returns the changed list.
Append to the wrong list while building a result.
java.explanation: Array indexes start at 0 and stop at length - 1. The condition i < arr.length visits the final valid index but stops before i becomes arr.length.

javascript.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 5
javascript.prompt: What should JavaScript code check about array methods?
choices: Know whether the method mutates the array or returns a new value.
Use nested indexes without checking the inner list length.
Assume every list method returns the changed list.
Append to the wrong list while building a result.
javascript.explanation: Some array methods change the array, such as push and pop. Others return new values. Knowing which one you are using prevents accidental shared-data bugs.

cpp.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 5
cpp.prompt: When is vector.at(index) useful in C++?
choices: Use it when an invalid index should throw a clear exception.
Use nested indexes without checking the inner list length.
Assume every list method returns the changed list.
Append to the wrong list while building a result.
cpp.explanation: vector.at(index) checks bounds and throws std::out_of_range for a bad index. Bracket indexing is faster-looking but unchecked, so a bad index becomes undefined behavior.

python.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 6
python.prompt: Why avoid removing items from a Python list while looping over it?
choices: Reset the result list inside the loop.
Avoid adding to or removing from a list while you loop over it. Build a new list of what you want to keep.
Use the item value as if it were the item index.
Ignore whether the data structure is fixed-size or growable.
python.explanation: Removing shifts later items left while the loop still advances. That can skip values that moved into the current position. Building a new list of kept items is usually clearer.

java.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 6
java.prompt: Why is `arr[arr.length]` invalid for every Java array?
choices: Reset the result list inside the loop.
`arr.length` is one past the final valid index.
Use the item value as if it were the item index.
Ignore whether the data structure is fixed-size or growable.
java.explanation: If arr.length is 3, the valid indexes are 0, 1, and 2. arr[arr.length] asks for arr[3], which is one past the allocated slots.

javascript.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 6
javascript.prompt: What do JavaScript arrays preserve about their values?
choices: Reset the result list inside the loop.
Store ordered values and access them by index.
Use the item value as if it were the item index.
Ignore whether the data structure is fixed-size or growable.
javascript.explanation: Arrays preserve order. That lets code read values by position, loop through them in sequence, and add or remove items at known places.

cpp.title: Lists / Arrays concept check 6
cpp.prompt: When would C++ code choose vector instead of a fixed array?
choices: Reset the result list inside the loop.
Store ordered elements in arrays and vectors.
Use the item value as if it were the item index.
Ignore whether the data structure is fixed-size or growable.
cpp.explanation: Choose vector when the number of elements may grow or shrink. A fixed array works when the size is known and should not change.
